Phase Transition for Budgeted Multi-Agent Synergy

Bang Liu bang.liu@umontreal.ca Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Operations Research Affiliation: Université de Montréal & Mila - Quebec AI Institute Affiliation: Montreal, QC, Canada    Linglong Kong lkong@ualberta.ca Affiliation: Department of Mathematical & Statistical Science Affiliation: University of Alberta, AB, Canada    Jian Pei j.pei@duke.edu Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Duke University, NC, United States
Abstract

Multi-agent systems can improve reliability, yet under a fixed inference budget they often help, saturate, or even collapse. We develop a deliberately minimal and calibratable theory that predicts these regimes from three binding constraints of modern agent stacks: finite context windows, lossy inter-agent communication, and shared failures among similar agents. Each leaf agent is summarized by a compute–performance scaling exponent β\beta; communication is captured by a message-length fidelity curve γ⁡(m)\gamma(m); dependence is captured by an effective shared-error correlation ρ\rho; and a context window WW imposes hard fan-in limits that make hierarchy necessary. For binary success/failure tasks with majority aggregation, we prove a sharp phase transition for deep bb-ary trees with correlated inputs and lossy communication: a single scalar αρ\alpha_{\rho} (combining γ⁡(m)\gamma(m), ρ\rho, and fan-in bb) determines whether weak signal is amplified to a nontrivial fixed point or washed out to chance. In the amplifying regime, we derive an organization exponent ss and show that budgeted synergy, i.e., outperforming the best single agent under the same total budget, occurs exactly when s>βs>\beta, yielding closed-form compute allocation rules and explicit budget thresholds. We further characterize saturation via a mixing depth and provide a conservative clipped predictor that remains accurate across growth and saturation. A continuous-performance warm-up gives closed-form risks for star, chain, and tree organizations, making correlation- and communication-induced floors explicit and exposing the core design trade-offs in a smooth setting. Finally, we validate the predicted phase boundaries in controlled synthetic simulations and show how the same mechanisms explain the dominant bottlenecks reported in recent large-scale matched-budget studies of LLM agent-system scaling, including context saturation, subcritical error cascades, and diminishing returns at strong baselines.

keywords
Budgeted Multi-Agent Synergy, Phase Transition, Shared-failure Correlation, Communication Bottlenecks, Finite Context Windows

1 Introduction

Multi-agent systems are often sold as a reliability primitive: if a single agent is fallible, run many agents, let them interact, and aggregate their outputs. Under a fixed inference budget, however, multi-agent coordination is not reliably beneficial. The same additional agents that sometimes improve performance can also yield saturation or outright degradation. This paper develops a predictive theory of this brittleness: when multi-agent organization produces budgeted synergy (i.e., outperforming any single agent under the same budget) and when scaling out must fail.

The LLM era has made the phenomenon impossible to ignore. It is now routine to instantiate multiple LLM-based agents, assign roles, and coordinate them through discussion, critique, or voting in “agent societies” and orchestration toolkits (Brown et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024). The underlying intuition is classical: ensembling can reduce error (Breiman, 1996; Freund and Schapire, 1997; Dietterich, 2000), and interaction protocols such as debate or amplification aim to turn many weak judgments into a stronger one (Irving et al., 2018; Christiano et al., 2018; Du et al., 2024). At the same time, controlled matched-budget evaluations increasingly report strong task- and topology-dependence, including regimes where multi-agent variants degrade once coordination overhead and information loss dominate (Kim et al., 2025).

Our starting point is that these failures are not implementation accidents but structural consequences of three constraints that repeatedly bind in modern agent stacks. First, agent errors are not independent: many instances derived from the same base model and prompt share failure modes, producing “groupthink” rather than error cancellation. Second, coordination is communication-limited: as systems scale, agents must compress reasoning into bounded-length messages, and this loss compounds across layers. Third, coordination is context-limited: a central aggregator cannot read arbitrarily many messages under a finite context window, so naive scale-out saturates structurally. Recent work on large-population collaboration and topology learning highlights the same bottleneck: token and context limits are often the binding resource (Qian et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024).

Today, agent-system design still largely proceeds by heuristics: choose a topology, message format, and number of agents, then iterate. In spirit, this resembles the hand-crafted feature engineering era of machine learning: powerful components exist, but system-level behavior depends on ad hoc choices and expensive trial-and-error. Our goal is to push multi-agent design toward an “agentic intelligence from first principles” style: make the dominant constraints explicit, explain why scaling out works or fails, and derive sharp, quantitative regime boundaries—in particular, a phase transition for budgeted multi-agent synergy.

A minimal, calibratable coordination theory.

We develop a deliberately small framework that isolates the coordination bottlenecks above while remaining analytically tractable. The term agent is used abstractly: a black-box solver that, given a task instance and an allocated compute budget, produces an output that another component can consume (a decision, a score, or an mm-token message). This deliberately includes LLM-based agents as a primary motivating instance, because (i) tokens provide a natural budget unit, (ii) finite context windows induce hard fan-in constraints, and (iii) single-agent capability is often well described by compute scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). At the same time, the abstraction is broader than LLMs: none of the results relies on language as such, only on (a) how single-agent quality scales with compute, (b) how much usable information survives bounded-length communication, and (c) how strongly agents’ failures co-move.

By calibratable we do not mean a theory “about measurement.” We mean a coordination theory parameterized by a small set of environment-dependent effective quantities that can be estimated once (via targeted experiments) and then used to predict qualitative regimes. Concretely, the framework is driven by single-agent scaling (exponent β\beta), communication fidelity as a function of message length (e.g., γ⁡(m)\gamma(m)), shared-failure correlation (ρ\rho), and the context window constraint (WW), together with a total budget BB that fixes the scale-up/scale-out trade-off. These parameters are not claimed to capture every detail of a real agent stack; they form a minimal interface for diagnosing which constraint is binding and for predicting when organization helps, saturates, or fails.

Phase transition for budgeted multi-agent synergy.

Within this framework we analyze three canonical organizations: star (central aggregation), chain (sequential handoff), and hierarchical tree. Our main results characterize when hierarchy is viable and when it is provably counterproductive. For binary success/failure tasks with majority aggregation, we prove a sharp amplification–collapse transition for deep trees: a scalar αρ\alpha_{\rho} (combining communication fidelity, correlation, and fan-in) determines whether weak signal amplifies across layers or is washed out to chance, in the spirit of reconstruction thresholds in noisy broadcasting on trees (Evans et al., 2000; Mossel, 2001; Kesten and Stigum, 1966). In the amplifying regime, we derive an organization exponent ss governing growth with the number of leaves and show that budgeted synergy in the growth range occurs exactly when s>βs>\beta, yielding closed-form compute allocation and explicit budget thresholds. We also characterize finite-depth saturation via a nontrivial fixed point and mixing-depth guarantees. Finally, we make precise why topology becomes decisive only because constraints bind: absent context limits, central aggregation is information-dominant (data processing inequality) (Cover and Thomas, 2006), and hierarchy is valuable only insofar as it bypasses fan-in limits without crossing into the collapsing regime.

Beyond the binary core, a continuous-performance warm-up yields closed-form risks for star/chain/tree organizations and makes correlation and communication floors explicit. We also translate theorems into design diagnostics (e.g., monotone communication design curves) and connect the predicted bottlenecks to recent controlled large-scale agent-scaling studies (Kim et al., 2025). Detailed calibration templates are collected in Appendix J.

Methodological stance: theory vs. benchmarking.

This is a theory paper: our aim is to delineate regimes of behavior and identify the mechanisms that govern when multi-agent systems help, saturate, or collapse under realistic constraints. Large-scale matched-budget evaluations with real LLM agent stacks are expensive and can be confounded by prompt engineering and rapidly changing model/tool ecosystems. Accordingly, we validate the sharp regime boundaries via controlled synthetic simulations (Section 7.2) that probe the theory under its own assumptions, and we use external controlled evidence (Kim et al., 2025) to show that the bottlenecks isolated by the theory (context saturation, subcritical collapse, and diminishing returns) are salient in modern deployments.

Organization.

Section 2 defines the framework, measurable parameters, and the budget and context constraints. Section 3 develops the continuous warm-up. Section 4 presents the binary theory, including the phase transition, small-signal amplification, and saturation. Section 5 compares topologies under context constraints and derives budget thresholds. Section 6 turns the theory into design diagnostics. Section 7 provides empirical touchpoints via external controlled evidence and synthetic sanity checks. We place detailed proofs and optional calibration/evaluation templates in the appendices.

2 Framework and Measurable Parameters

This section formalizes the abstraction used throughout the paper. We keep only three constraints that repeatedly bind in practice: finite context windows, lossy communication, and shared failures, and summarize the environment by a small set of quantities. These quantities play distinct roles: β\beta captures how a single agent improves with compute, γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) (or σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m)) captures what survives an mm-token message, and ρ\rho captures how correlated different agents’ errors are. Together with a total budget BB and a context window WW, they determine whether scaling out amplifies signal, saturates at a floor, or collapses.

We model a multi-agent system as a directed acyclic computation graph. Leaf nodes (agents) produce signals about a latent task variable YY; internal nodes receive messages from their children (possibly through a lossy channel) and apply an aggregation rule; the root output is the system prediction. Throughout, an agent is a black-box solver with an adjustable compute budget xx that emits a bounded-length output (a decision, a score, or an mm-token message). LLM-based agents are the primary motivating instance, but the framework only assumes a single-agent scaling curve, a communication-fidelity curve, and a shared-failure correlation.

2.1 Tasks and performance metrics

We study two task primitives that cover many MAS evaluations and isolate the coordination bottlenecks above. Binary success/failure captures accuracy-like outcomes (pass rates, accept/reject decisions). Continuous performance on [0,1][0,1] captures graded scoring or calibrated estimates and provides a smooth warm-up where many expressions admit closed forms. The continuous setting is not a substitute for the binary theory; it makes correlation and communication floors explicit without the nonlinearity introduced by majority vote.

Binary tasks.

Let Y∈{−1,+1}Y\in\{-1,+1\} denote the ground truth. A system outputs Y^∈{−1,+1}\widehat{Y}\in\{-1,+1\}. We measure performance through the bias

μ:=𝔼⁡[Y^​Y]∈[−1,1],Pr⁡(Y^=Y)=1+μ2.\mu\;:=\;\mathbb{E}[\widehat{Y}Y]\in[-1,1],\qquad\Pr(\widehat{Y}=Y)=\frac{1+\mu}{2}.

The bias μ\mu is convenient for multi-layer analysis because it composes cleanly under simple channel models and aggregation maps.

Continuous tasks.

Let Y∈[0,1]Y\in[0,1] and a system output Y^∈[0,1]\widehat{Y}\in[0,1]. We use mean squared error (MSE)

v:=𝔼⁡[(Y^−Y)2],v\;:=\;\mathbb{E}\big[(\widehat{Y}-Y)^{2}\big],

and occasionally report a bounded performance score such as Perf=1/(1+v)\mathrm{Perf}=1/(1+v), which is monotone in vv. The continuous analysis yields explicit floors; the binary analysis additionally introduces a sharp amplification–collapse transition.

2.2 Single-agent capability and scaling

Our central comparison is fixed-budget: the same total budget BB can be spent on fewer stronger agents (scale up) or more weaker agents (scale out). We model per-leaf compute by a single knob x≥0x\geq 0. In an LLM agent, xx can represent a token budget for reasoning, the number of samples or self-consistency votes, the number of tool calls, or any additive resource that trades off against parallelism.

We summarize the effect of compute via a single-agent scaling law, motivated by empirical power-law relations between performance and compute observed for large language models and related systems (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). For binary tasks, a leaf with compute xx produces a vote Y^\widehat{Y} with bias

μ0​(x)=g​(x),\mu_{0}(x)=g(x),

where g⁡(⋅)g(\cdot) is increasing and typically exhibits diminishing returns. For continuous tasks, a leaf produces an estimate XX with conditional variance v0​(x)v_{0}(x), where v0​(⋅)v_{0}(\cdot) decreases with xx.

In our main theorems, we work in a regime where these functions are well-approximated by power laws:

Binary: g⁡(x)≈k​xβ(small-signal regime),\displaystyle g(x)\approx k\,x^{\beta}\quad\text{(small-signal regime)}, (1)
Continuous: v0​(x)≈c​x−β,\displaystyle v_{0}(x)\approx c\,x^{-\beta}, (2)

with constants k,c>0k,c>0 and a single-agent scaling exponent β>0\beta>0. The exponent β\beta is not a universal constant. It depends on the model, prompting, tools, and the task family, and it is intended to be measured.

2.3 Communication as a controllable lossy channel

Agents coordinate through messages. Our analysis uses a compact abstraction of how message length affects what downstream nodes can reliably use.

We model each edge as a channel controlled by a message length parameter mm (in tokens). Longer messages generally preserve more usable information, but they also cost more budget and reduce feasible fan-in under a finite context window.

Binary: an effective bit channel.

For binary tasks and majority-style protocols, it is natural to treat each child as intending to transmit a single bit of information (its vote or decision), encoded into a message of length mm. We model the receiver’s decoded bit as passing through a binary symmetric channel (BSC) with reliability γ⁡(m)∈(0,1]\gamma(m)\in(0,1]: if a child has bias μ\mu relative to YY, then after transmission the received bit has bias γ⁡(m)​μ\gamma(m)\mu. Equivalently, γ⁡(m)=1−2​ϵ​(m)\gamma(m)=1-2\epsilon(m) where ϵ⁡(m)\epsilon(m) is an effective flip probability.

Continuous: additive distortion.

For continuous tasks, we model transmission as additive zero-mean distortion,

X~=X+η,𝔼⁡[η]=0,Var⁡(η)=σc2​(m),\widetilde{X}=X+\eta,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\eta]=0,\quad\mathrm{Var}(\eta)=\sigma_{c}^{2}(m),

where σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m) decreases with mm. This captures compression loss, imperfect interpretation, and degradation introduced by summarization or constrained prompts.

The intent is not to claim that real messages are literally bits or Gaussian perturbations, but to represent an effective fidelity curve as a function of mm. In particular, γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) or σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m) can be estimated by simple encode–decode experiments at the same message length.

2.4 Shared-failure correlation and the ρ\rho model

A key departure from idealized ensemble analyses is that agent errors are not independent, even though many ensemble gains are easiest to analyze under weak dependence assumptions (Dietterich, 2000; Germain et al., 2015). Agents instantiated from the same base model and prompt often share systematic error modes, which can dominate any aggregation gain. We capture this effect with a single, measurable correlation parameter ρ∈[0,1)\rho\in[0,1).

Binary: correlation of signed correctness.

For a leaf vote Y^i\widehat{Y}_{i}, define the signed correctness variable

Si:=Y^i​Y∈{−1,+1}.S_{i}:=\widehat{Y}_{i}Y\in\{-1,+1\}.

Then 𝔼⁡[Si]=μ0\mathbb{E}[S_{i}]=\mu_{0}, and we define

ρ:=Corr⁡(Si,Sj),i≠j,\rho\;:=\;\mathrm{Corr}(S_{i},S_{j}),\qquad i\neq j,

estimated empirically by averaging pairwise correlations across tasks and agent instances. Here ii and jj index two agent instances whose outputs are aggregated together: for a star this is any pair of leaves; for a tree it should be interpreted as the sibling correlation at an internal node. In practice the effective correlation can depend on depth, heterogeneity, or the message schema; for tractability we treat ρ\rho as a depth-independent effective parameter and return to extensions in Section 8. Intuitively, ρ=0\rho=0 corresponds to independent errors, while ρ\rho close to 1 indicates near-perfect groupthink.

For analysis, we use a concrete generative model that matches this definition exactly. At each aggregation node, with probability ρ\rho the children share a common “mode” (their signed correctness variables are identical), and with probability 1−ρ1-\rho they are conditionally independent given YY. This model produces the same pairwise correlation ρ\rho while remaining analytically tractable and yields a closed-form correlated aggregation map used throughout the paper.

Continuous: correlated residuals.

For continuous outputs XiX_{i}, define residuals Ei:=Xi−YE_{i}:=X_{i}-Y. We use the standard equal-correlation model

Var⁡(Ei)=v,Cov⁡(Ei,Ej)=ρ​v,i≠j,\mathrm{Var}(E_{i})=v,\qquad\mathrm{Cov}(E_{i},E_{j})=\rho v,\quad i\neq j,

which makes correlation floors explicit and leads to closed-form recursions in Section 3. The same ρ\rho can be estimated by pairwise residual correlations.

Why a single parameter is useful.

Real systems may have richer dependence structure than a single coefficient. The intent here is not to model all dependence, but to isolate the dominant failure direction: shared errors. As we show later, this single parameter already shifts phase boundaries and imposes aggregation floors that are otherwise difficult to diagnose.

2.5 Budget and context constraints

Our central comparison is fixed-budget: a multi-agent system should be judged against the best single-agent baseline under the same total cost. We therefore make computation and communication costs explicit.

Budget.

Let BB denote the total available budget. In token-based LLM systems, a natural accounting unit is tokens, including both generated tokens and tokens processed as input. Our theory is compatible with other budget units (time, API cost, calls), as long as they are additive and comparable across designs.

We separate two costs:

  • •

    Leaf computation: each leaf agent is allocated compute xx.

  • •

    Communication: each edge transmits a message of length mm tokens.

To keep the model simple, we account a per-edge cost proportional to mm. A useful approximation in token-based systems is

edge cost≈2​m,\text{edge cost}\approx 2m,

representing mm tokens produced by the sender and mm tokens read by the receiver.

Context window as a fan-in constraint.

Let WW denote the maximum number of tokens that an internal node can read and process. If each incoming message has length mm, then any aggregation node can read at most

fan-in≤⌊Wm⌋.\text{fan-in}\leq\Big\lfloor\frac{W}{m}\Big\rfloor.

This inequality is the reason depth matters: a star is capped by N≤⌊W/m⌋N\leq\lfloor W/m\rfloor leaves, while a tree can scale to N=bLN=b^{L} leaves by distributing the fan-in constraint across levels.

Topology-specific cost summaries.

Let NN be the number of leaves. Under the accounting above:

  • •

    Star: Cstar​(N,x,m)≈N⁡(x+2​m)C_{\text{star}}(N,x,m)\approx N(x+2m), with feasibility constraint N​m≤WNm\leq W.

  • •

    Chain: for length LL, Cchain​(L,x,m)≈(L+1)​x+2​m​LC_{\text{chain}}(L,x,m)\approx(L+1)x+2mL (assuming each handoff step runs an agent with compute x, e.g., one model call), with feasibility constraint m≤Wm\leq W (usually nonbinding).

  • •

    Tree: for a full bb-ary tree of depth LL with N=bLN=b^{L} leaves, the number of edges is

    E=b⋅N−1b−1,E=b\cdot\frac{N-1}{b-1},

    so Ctree​(b,L,x,m)≈N​x+2​m​EC_{\text{tree}}(b,L,x,m)\approx Nx+2mE. It is convenient to write this as a per-leaf cost:

    Ctree​(b,L,x,m)≈N⁡(x+c0​(b,m)),c0​(b,m):=2​m​bb−1,C_{\text{tree}}(b,L,x,m)\approx N\big(x+c_{0}(b,m)\big),\qquad c_{0}(b,m):=2m\frac{b}{b-1},

    subject to the fan-in feasibility b​m≤Wbm\leq W. Alternative accounting (templating overheads, parsing costs, asymmetric protocols) rescales c0​(b,m)c_{0}(b,m) and can be treated as an implementation constant.

This approximation isolates the basic trade-off: increasing mm can improve fidelity, but it also increases coordination cost and reduces the number of leaves affordable under BB.

2.6 Topologies and protocols

A topology specifies how information flows; a protocol specifies what each node does with the information it receives. We keep protocols deliberately simple to make the effect of constraints and scaling transparent. In particular, we focus on three canonical organizations that recur in practice and isolate the key trade-offs: star, chain, and hierarchical tree (Figure 1).

Star.

Leaves transmit their outputs directly to a central aggregator. Star avoids multi-hop loss, but it concentrates fan-in at one node and therefore saturates at N≈W/mN\approx W/m leaves regardless of budget.

Chain.

Outputs are passed sequentially through LL steps. Chains avoid fan-in bottlenecks but repeatedly retransmit information; without new evidence injected along the path, each step can only preserve or degrade the signal.

Hierarchical tree.

A tree distributes aggregation across many small nodes. Each internal node aggregates bb child messages and forwards a summary upward, enforcing b​m≤Wbm\leq W locally and enabling many more leaves. The cost is multi-hop communication and repeated aggregation, so performance hinges on whether amplification dominates compounding loss and correlation.

Why focus on star, chain, and tree?

These motifs capture the dominant structural trade-offs induced by finite context and imperfect coordination. Star minimizes depth but is capped by a global fan-in constraint N​m≤WNm\leq W. Chain removes fan-in limits but maximizes the number of lossy transmissions. Trees are the simplest family that bypasses the fan-in cap (b​m≤Wbm\leq W locally) while still aggregating many signals; this is precisely the setting in which phase transitions and budget thresholds emerge.

It is also useful to view more general feed-forward organizations through these motifs. With a finite context window, every node can only aggregate a bounded number of incoming messages, i.e., each local computation is an in-star with fan-in at most ⌊W/m⌋\lfloor W/m\rfloor. Globally, any connected directed acyclic communication graph contains a spanning arborescence that routes leaf information to the output; star and chain are the two extreme cases (depth 11 versus fan-in 11), and bounded-fan-in trees are the minimal structure that scales beyond the star’s context cap. Additional edges or multi-round interaction are valuable mainly when they effectively change the measurable parameters, for example by improving effective fidelity through redundancy or by reducing effective correlation through independent verification, rather than by rerouting the same information along multiple dependent paths.

Aggregation rules.

We analyze majority vote at internal nodes for binary tasks (ties are avoided by choosing odd fan-in) and averaging for continuous tasks (the MSE-optimal linear unbiased aggregator under equal-variance equal-correlation assumptions). More sophisticated protocols (critique, verification, debate) can be interpreted in our framework as mechanisms that effectively increase communication fidelity or reduce shared-error correlation. We return to this connection in the discussion.

2.7 What is measurable and how to measure it

The framework is parameterized by a small set of environment-dependent quantities. Table 1 summarizes their meaning and outlines how one might estimate them in a specific model–task setting. These estimates are optional: the theoretical results that follow hold given β\beta, ρ\rho, and the communication curves, while calibration is a way to connect the regime predictions back to concrete agent stacks at a coarse level.

Sections 3–6 use these parameters to derive correlation/communication floors, a binary amplification–collapse phase transition, and budget-dependent topology comparisons.

3 Continuous Warm-up: Averaging Under Correlation and Communication Noise

We begin with a continuous-performance setting in which agents estimate a scalar target Y∈[0,1]Y\in[0,1] and performance is measured by mean squared error (MSE). This warm-up makes the basic organization trade-offs transparent in closed form: averaging reduces independent noise, shared errors impose floors, and communication loss introduces additional distortion. Throughout we adopt the framework of Section 2 and use averaging at internal nodes, which is the natural choice under squared loss and symmetric noise assumptions.

Although we phrase the warm-up as each leaf producing an estimate of the same latent YY, it should be read as an abstraction of role-specialized pipelines. A child agent may solve a subtask and transmit an mm-token message; XiX_{i} denotes the effective scalar contribution about the downstream target that the parent can decode from that message. Role heterogeneity then enters through the effective parameters (ρ\rho and σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m) or γ⁡(m)\gamma(m)); we return to richer semantics and extensions in Section 8.

3.1 Model assumptions for the continuous setting

Let Y∈[0,1]Y\in[0,1] denote the latent truth and let each leaf output an estimate X∈[0,1]X\in[0,1]. To keep the warm-up focused on organization rather than estimator bias, we assume leaf estimates are conditionally unbiased:

𝔼⁡[X∣Y]=Y.\mathbb{E}[X\mid Y]=Y.

We write the leaf residual as E:=X−YE:=X-Y, so 𝔼⁡[E∣Y]=0\mathbb{E}[E\mid Y]=0. Leaf quality is summarized by the conditional MSE,

v0​(x):=𝔼⁡[(X−Y)2]=𝔼⁡[E2],v_{0}(x):=\mathbb{E}\big[(X-Y)^{2}\big]=\mathbb{E}\big[E^{2}\big],

which depends on per-leaf compute xx. In the scaling regime of interest we model

v0​(x)≈c​x−β,v_{0}(x)\approx c\,x^{-\beta}, (3)

with constants c>0c>0 and β>0\beta>0, as introduced in Section 2.2.

Communication distortion.

An estimate sent across an edge as a message of length mm is received with additive distortion:

X~=X+η,𝔼⁡[η]=0,Var⁡(η)=σc2​(m),\widetilde{X}=X+\eta,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\eta]=0,\quad\mathrm{Var}(\eta)=\sigma_{c}^{2}(m), (4)

where σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m) decreases with mm. We treat the channel noise variables η\eta as independent across edges and independent of YY. This is a compact abstraction of imperfect summarization, constrained prompts, and the general fact that receivers do not reconstruct sender information perfectly.

Shared errors as residual correlation.

Within any aggregation group, child residuals are not assumed independent. Instead, we use an equal-correlation model: for children i≠ji\neq j with residuals Ei,EjE_{i},E_{j},

Var⁡(Ei)=v,Cov⁡(Ei,Ej)=ρ​v,\mathrm{Var}(E_{i})=v,\qquad\mathrm{Cov}(E_{i},E_{j})=\rho v, (5)

where ρ∈[0,1)\rho\in[0,1) is the correlation coefficient. This matches the intended interpretation of ρ\rho as a measurable “shared-failure” strength: ρ=0\rho=0 corresponds to independent residuals, while ρ\rho near 1 indicates strong groupthink.

Aggregation by averaging.

An internal node with fan-in bb receives X~1,…,X~b\widetilde{X}_{1},\dots,\widetilde{X}_{b} and outputs the average

Y^=1b​∑i=1bX~i.\widehat{Y}=\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}\widetilde{X}_{i}. (6)

Under the symmetry assumptions above, this is the MSE-optimal linear unbiased aggregator.

3.2 Closed-form risk for star, chain, and tree

We now derive exact MSE expressions (or recursions) for the three canonical topologies. These formulas already reveal three key messages: star saturates under context constraints, chains compound loss, and trees trade scale for multi-hop noise.

Star.

Consider a star with NN leaves feeding a single aggregator. Each leaf sends a length-mm message, so the aggregator is feasible only if N​m≤WNm\leq W. Let v0v_{0} denote the leaf MSE (for a given compute allocation xx) and let ρ\rho denote the pairwise residual correlation within this aggregation group. After one hop, each received estimate has residual E~i=(Xi−Y)+ηi\widetilde{E}_{i}=(X_{i}-Y)+\eta_{i}, with

Var⁡(E~i)=v0+σc2​(m),Cov⁡(E~i,E~j)=ρ​v0.\mathrm{Var}(\widetilde{E}_{i})=v_{0}+\sigma_{c}^{2}(m),\qquad\mathrm{Cov}(\widetilde{E}_{i},\widetilde{E}_{j})=\rho v_{0}.

The star output is the average of the received values, so the MSE is

vstar​(N)=𝔼⁡[(Y^−Y)2]=v0​(1+(N−1)​ρ)N+σc2​(m)N.v_{\text{star}}(N)=\mathbb{E}\big[(\widehat{Y}-Y)^{2}\big]=\frac{v_{0}\big(1+(N-1)\rho\big)}{N}+\frac{\sigma_{c}^{2}(m)}{N}. (7)

If NN could grow arbitrarily, the channel noise term σc2​(m)/N\sigma_{c}^{2}(m)/N would vanish. However, correlation produces an irreducible floor:

vstar​(N)→ρ​v0as ​N→∞​ (for fixed ​v0​).v_{\text{star}}(N)\ \to\ \rho v_{0}\qquad\text{as }N\to\infty\text{ (for fixed }v_{0}\text{)}.

Thus, even perfect communication cannot eliminate a globally shared residual component. In practice, the context constraint N​m≤WNm\leq W prevents NN from growing with budget once mm is fixed, which is why star organizations often stop improving beyond a modest scale.

Chain.

Consider a chain of length LL, where an estimate is handed off sequentially through LL communication steps, each of length mm, without introducing new independent evidence. Starting from a leaf estimate with MSE v0v_{0}, each hop adds independent distortion variance σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m). Thus,

vchain​(L)=v0+L​σc2​(m).v_{\text{chain}}(L)=v_{0}+L\,\sigma_{c}^{2}(m). (8)

Equation (8) isolates the unavoidable cost of multi-hop relay communication: if intermediate nodes primarily re-encode the same information (no new independent evidence), each hop injects distortion and MSE grows linearly in LL. Pipeline-style chains can still be beneficial when each stage performs additional computation or incorporates new information; in that case, the estimation error may decrease across stages, but the same σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m) term captures a communication bottleneck that accumulates with depth and must be outweighed by per-stage gains.

Hierarchical tree.

Consider a full bb-ary tree with depth LL, where each internal node averages its bb children. Let vtv_{t} denote the MSE of a node output at level tt (leaves are t=0t=0; the root is t=Lt=L). We assume that at each aggregation node, the bb child residuals satisfy the equal-correlation model (5) with coefficient ρ\rho, and that channel noise on incoming edges is independent.

A parent receives X~i=Xi+ηi\widetilde{X}_{i}=X_{i}+\eta_{i} from each child, so each received residual has variance vt+σc2​(m)v_{t}+\sigma_{c}^{2}(m), while covariances remain ρ​vt\rho v_{t} because the channel noises are independent. Averaging (6) yields the recursion

vt+1=a​vt+σc2​(m)b,a:=1+(b−1)​ρb=ρ+1−ρb.v_{t+1}=a\,v_{t}+\frac{\sigma_{c}^{2}(m)}{b},\qquad a:=\frac{1+(b-1)\rho}{b}=\rho+\frac{1-\rho}{b}. (9)

vL=aL​v0+σc2​(m)b⋅1−aL1−a.v_{L}=a^{L}v_{0}+\frac{\sigma_{c}^{2}(m)}{b}\cdot\frac{1-a^{L}}{1-a}. (10)

This is the statistical benefit of hierarchy: averaging repeatedly reduces the variance of what is being passed upward. The second term is the cost: each level injects fresh communication distortion, which accumulates into an error floor described next.

3.3 Saturation floors and mixing depth

Equation (10) exposes a sharp and practical phenomenon: deeper trees do not improve indefinitely. Even if leaves become arbitrarily accurate, repeated communication loss produces a floor. Figure 3 illustrates the typical behavior: vLv_{L} shrinks rapidly with depth at first (roughly at rate aLa^{L}) and then saturates at the floor v⋆v^{\star} determined by σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m), bb, and ρ\rho.

For ρ<1\rho<1 we have a<1a<1, and therefore aL→0a^{L}\to 0 as L→∞L\to\infty. Taking limits in (10) yields

v⋆​(b,m,ρ):=limL→∞vL=σc2​(m)b⁡(1−a)=σc2​(m)(b−1)​(1−ρ).v^{\star}(b,m,\rho):=\lim_{L\to\infty}v_{L}=\frac{\sigma_{c}^{2}(m)}{b(1-a)}=\frac{\sigma_{c}^{2}(m)}{(b-1)(1-\rho)}. (11)

This expression cleanly separates the levers available to a designer:

  • •

    Increasing message length mm decreases σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m), lowering the floor.

  • •

    Increasing fan-in bb lowers the floor approximately as 1/(b−1)1/(b-1), but bb is limited by b​m≤Wbm\leq W.

  • •

    Reducing shared correlation ρ\rho lowers the floor and also accelerates convergence (since aa decreases).

The recursion (9) is linear, so convergence to the floor is explicit:

vL−v⋆=aL​(v0−v⋆).v_{L}-v^{\star}=a^{L}\,(v_{0}-v^{\star}). (12)

Thus, to achieve a relative tolerance vL≤(1+ε)​v⋆v_{L}\leq(1+\varepsilon)v^{\star} when v0>v⋆v_{0}>v^{\star}, it suffices to choose

L≥⌈log⁡((v0−v⋆)/(ε​v⋆))log⁡(1/a)⌉.L\ \geq\ \left\lceil\frac{\log\big((v_{0}-v^{\star})/(\varepsilon v^{\star})\big)}{\log(1/a)}\right\rceil. (13)

Equation (13) is the continuous analogue of the “mixing depth” results we prove for binary trees later. It is also a direct design rule: beyond a certain depth, additional leaves yield negligible improvement unless the designer reduces the floor by improving communication or reducing correlation.

A note on when deeper is worse.

If leaves are already more accurate than the floor (i.e., v0<v⋆v_{0}<v^{\star}), then (10) implies that increasing depth moves error upward toward v⋆v^{\star}. In that regime, deeper hierarchies are counterproductive unless they come with reduced σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m) or reduced ρ\rho. This observation will reappear in the binary setting as a saturation effect: once the system has reached its fixed point, additional scale should be spent on changing the communication or correlation regime rather than adding depth.

3.5 Design implications and a bridge to the binary analysis

The continuous warm-up already exposes the structural trade-offs we will reuse in the binary theory. Absent a binding context constraint, star aggregation is information-dominant because it avoids multi-hop loss; trees are useful primarily as a way to bypass the fan-in limit N​m≤WNm\leq W by enforcing b​m≤Wbm\leq W locally, at the cost of repeated communication. Both correlation and communication loss induce explicit performance floors, so scale-out can stall early when ρ\rho is large or messages are too short. In the growth regime under a fixed budget, the key comparison is exponent versus exponent: whether the organization exponent beats the single-agent scaling exponent.

The binary case is qualitatively different. Averaging is linear, so errors evolve smoothly toward an explicit floor. Majority vote discards magnitude and retains only a sign; when the incoming signal is too weak relative to noise and correlation, repeated majority aggregation can wash out information rather than denoise it. Section 4 formalizes this amplification–collapse transition and shows how the same measurable quantities (ρ\rho, message length mm, fan-in bb, and budget allocation) determine whether organization helps or hurts on success/failure tasks.

4 Binary Core: Majority Aggregation and Phase Transitions

Binary success/failure tasks behave differently from the continuous warm-up because majority vote discards magnitude information and retains only a sign. That nonlinearity can either amplify weak signal across layers or wash it out entirely. As a result, hierarchical organization exhibits a sharp tipping point: below a threshold, deeper trees collapse to chance; above it, depth improves accuracy until it saturates.

Real multi-agent pipelines often mix graded intermediate signals (scores, confidences, rankings) with hard decisions (accept/reject, pass/fail). We therefore view the continuous and binary analyses as two canonical primitives that appear within richer protocols; the same measurable constraints (communication fidelity, shared failures, and context-limited fan-in) govern both.

4.1 Majority maps and correlated aggregation

From leaf votes to bias.

Recall from Section 2.1 that for a binary task Y∈{−1,+1}Y\in\{-1,+1\}, we evaluate an output Y^∈{−1,+1}\widehat{Y}\in\{-1,+1\} through the bias

μ:=𝔼⁡[Y^​Y],Pr⁡(Y^=Y)=1+μ2.\mu:=\mathbb{E}[\widehat{Y}Y],\qquad\Pr(\widehat{Y}=Y)=\frac{1+\mu}{2}.

In a tree, each internal node receives bb child votes and outputs an aggregated vote. To analyze such systems, we need to understand how bias transforms through one aggregation step.

Majority aggregation map.

Let b≥3b\geq 3 be an odd integer and let V1,…,Vb∈{−1,+1}V_{1},\dots,V_{b}\in\{-1,+1\} be i.i.d. child votes with

For odd b≥3b\geq 3, the map fb:[−1,1]→[−1,1]f_{b}:[-1,1]\to[-1,1] satisfies:

Proof sketch.

Because TT is concave with T⁡(0)=0T(0)=0, the ratio r⁡(u):=T⁡(u)/ur(u):=T(u)/u is nonincreasing on u∈(0,1]u\in(0,1]. Its limit at the origin is r⁡(0+)=T′​(0)=αρr(0^{+})=T^{\prime}(0)=\alpha_{\rho}. If αρ≤1\alpha_{\rho}\leq 1, then T⁡(u)≤uT(u)\leq u for all u∈(0,1]u\in(0,1], so the recursion is monotone decreasing and must converge to a fixed point; the only possibility is 0. If αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1, then r⁡(0+)>1r(0^{+})>1, while r⁡(1)=T⁡(1)≤1r(1)=T(1)\leq 1 with strict inequality when γ<1\gamma<1. By monotonicity of rr, there is a unique uu where r⁡(u)=1r(u)=1, yielding a unique μ⋆\mu^{\star}. The sign of T⁡(u)−uT(u)-u implies the recursion moves toward μ⋆\mu^{\star} from any starting point. Full details are given in Appendix C. □\square

Connection to reconstruction thresholds.

In the classical broadcasting problem on trees with a binary symmetric channel (BSC) of second eigenvalue θ\theta, the Kesten–Stigum condition b​θ2>1b\theta^{2}>1 characterizes when the root remains reconstructable from the leaves (it is tight for the two-state symmetric model and, more generally, gives the Kesten–Stigum bound for Bayes-optimal reconstruction) (Kesten and Stigum, 1966; Evans et al., 2000; Mossel, 2001). Our condition αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1 plays an analogous role for the specific majority-based recursion under our correlated-input model and effective reliability γ⁡(m)\gamma(m): it is exactly the linear gain T′​(0)T^{\prime}(0) of the update map at the origin. We emphasize that αρ\alpha_{\rho} is estimator-dependent (majority rather than Bayes-optimal) and explicitly incorporates shared failures through ρ\rho.

What the threshold means in practice.

Theorem 4 clarifies why adding hierarchical structure is risky. In a supercritical regime, a tree can turn many weak votes into a strong decision and is robust to depth until it saturates. In a subcritical regime, depth destroys information: the system becomes less reliable as it grows. Both correlation (ρ\rho) and short messages (small γ⁡(m)\gamma(m)) push αρ\alpha_{\rho} downward, making collapse more likely. This matches the practitioner experience that groupthink and aggressive compression are the two most common reasons multi-agent scaling fails.

4.3 Small-signal amplification and the organization exponent ss

The phase transition determines whether deep organization is viable at all. When it is viable (αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1), the next question is how fast accuracy can grow with the number of leaves. This is where a simple exponent emerges.

Linear regime and a global upper bound.

Concavity of TT implies a strong inequality: the tangent line at the origin upper-bounds the entire map on [0,1][0,1],

T⁡(u)≤T′​(0)​u=αρ​u,u∈[0,1].T(u)\leq T^{\prime}(0)\,u=\alpha_{\rho}\,u,\qquad u\in[0,1]. (23)

Thus, for a depth-LL tree,

μL≤μ0​αρL.\mu_{L}\leq\mu_{0}\,\alpha_{\rho}^{L}. (24)

This bound is informative even when αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1: it tells us that exponential growth in depth is the fastest possible behavior in the small-signal regime.

To complement (24) we also need a lower bound showing that the upper bound is tight when signals remain small. Because TT is differentiable at 0, its local behavior is well-approximated by its derivative.

Fix b,ρ,γb,\rho,\gamma and let T​(u)=fb,ρ​(γ​u)T(u)=f_{b,\rho}(\gamma u) with αρ=T′​(0)\alpha_{\rho}=T^{\prime}(0). For any η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1), there exists δ=δ⁡(η,b,ρ,γ)∈(0,1]\delta=\delta(\eta;b,\rho,\gamma)\in(0,1] such that for all u∈[0,δ]u\in[0,\delta],

Consequently, if μ0​αρL≤δ\mu_{0}\,\alpha_{\rho}^{L}\leq\delta, then the depth-LL recursion satisfies

The upper bound is (23). For the lower bound, differentiability of TT at 0 implies T⁡(u)/u→αρT(u)/u\to\alpha_{\rho} as u↓0u\downarrow 0. For a full bb-ary tree of depth LL, the number of leaves is N=bLN=b^{L}. Theorem 5 implies that in the growth regime (before saturation),

μL≈μ0​αρL=μ0​Ns,s:=log⁡αρlog⁡b.\mu_{L}\approx\mu_{0}\,\alpha_{\rho}^{L}=\mu_{0}\,N^{s},\qquad s:=\frac{\log\alpha_{\rho}}{\log b}.

We call ss the organization exponent. It converts the per-layer gain αρ\alpha_{\rho} into a statement about how performance scales with the number of leaves under hierarchical aggregation.

This exponent is the main interface between organization and budget. Later, in Section 5, we compare ss to the single-agent scaling exponent β\beta to decide whether scale-out can beat scale-up under a fixed budget. At this stage, the key point is conceptual: ss increases with better communication (γ⁡(m)\gamma(m)), decreases with shared failures (ρ\rho), and is limited by fan-in through fb′​(0)f_{b}^{\prime}(0).

Small-signal amplification does not continue forever. Bias is bounded by 1, and communication loss and correlation prevent arbitrarily deep trees from achieving perfect accuracy unless the channel is lossless. Theorem 4 already tells us that in the supercritical regime the recursion converges to a fixed point μ⋆\mu^{\star}. In practice, we need two additional pieces of information: how quickly μt\mu_{t} approaches μ⋆\mu^{\star}, and how to build a design objective that remains accurate across both growth and saturation regimes.

Because TT is concave and T⁡(μ⋆)=μ⋆T(\mu^{\star})=\mu^{\star}, the slope at the fixed point satisfies T′​(μ⋆)≤1T^{\prime}(\mu^{\star})\leq 1, with strict inequality whenever γ<1\gamma<1 or ρ<1\rho<1. Theorem 6 (Finite-depth convergence to the fixed point).

Assume αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1 and ρ∈[0,1)\rho\in[0,1). Let μ⋆∈(0,1]\mu^{\star}\in(0,1] be the unique fixed point of TT from Theorem 4. For any ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), there exists a finite depth Lmix​(ε)L_{\mathrm{mix}}(\varepsilon) such that

There are two phases. First, while μt\mu_{t} is small, the map grows approximately linearly with factor αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1, so reaching a constant-size neighborhood of μ⋆\mu^{\star} takes O⁡(log⁡(1/μ0))O(\log(1/\mu_{0})) steps. The results above suggest a simple approximation that is both interpretable and safe: use the small-signal prediction μ0​αρL\mu_{0}\alpha_{\rho}^{L} when it is below the saturation point, and clip it at μ⋆\mu^{\star} otherwise:

μ^L:=min⁡{μ⋆,μ0​αρL}.\widehat{\mu}_{L}:=\min\big\{\mu^{\star},\ \mu_{0}\,\alpha_{\rho}^{L}\big\}. (27)

The clipped objective captures the two dominant regimes with a single expression. Design takeaway.

Equation (27) makes a practical point precise. In the supercritical regime, adding depth and leaves helps only until the system approaches μ⋆\mu^{\star}. Beyond that point, additional budget should be spent on changing μ⋆\mu^{\star} itself, which requires improving communication fidelity (increasing γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) by using longer messages) or reducing shared-error correlation ρ\rho (increasing diversity or adding verification). In the subcritical regime, adding depth is actively harmful; the only viable route to scale-out is to move the system across the threshold αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1 by improving mm, reducing ρ\rho, or increasing fan-in bb within the context constraint.

Section 5 uses the organization exponent ss, the threshold αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1, and the clipped objective (27) to derive topology and budget phase diagrams under context limits. Section 6 turns these results into a theory-guided design algorithm that outputs monotone communication design curves and compute allocations under a fixed budget.

5 Topology and Budget Phase Diagrams

Sections 3–4 characterized how information transforms through a single aggregation layer. This section turns those layer-wise results into system-level guidance: when centralized aggregation (star) is feasible, when hierarchy (tree) is necessary, and how these choices interact with a fixed budget BB under a context window constraint WW. The resulting phase diagrams organize a large design space into regimes governed by the environment parameters of Section 2 (the single-agent scaling exponent β\beta, shared-failure correlation ρ\rho, and communication fidelity γ⁡(m)\gamma(m)) together with the context constraint WW.

We focus on the binary setting and use the recursion and organization exponent developed in Section 4; when helpful, we connect back to the continuous warm-up to build intuition.

5.1 Star as an upper bound without constraints

A recurring empirical pattern is that hierarchies sometimes outperform naive centralization. It is tempting to interpret this as “hierarchy is intrinsically better.” Without constraints, that interpretation is false. A star is not merely a particular topology; it is the topology that gives the decision rule access to all leaf information in a single place. Any hierarchy that compresses information on the way up can only discard information, not create it (Cover and Thomas, 2006).

We formalize this point in an intentionally general way, independent of the details of the aggregation rule.

Proposition 7 (Centralization dominates under unlimited context).

Let X=(X1,…,XN)X=(X_{1},\dots,X_{N}) denote the collection of all leaf messages (or leaf outputs) generated in response to a task with truth label YY. Consider any multi-agent protocol on any directed acyclic topology such that the root ultimately observes a variable ZZ that is a (possibly randomized) function of XX with randomness independent of YY. Then for any loss ℓ⁡(Y^,Y)\ell(\widehat{Y},Y),

infY^=ϕ⁡(Z)𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Y^,Y)]≥infY^=ψ⁡(X)𝔼⁡[ℓ⁡(Y^,Y)].\inf_{\widehat{Y}=\phi(Z)}\mathbb{E}[\ell(\widehat{Y},Y)]\;\geq\;\inf_{\widehat{Y}=\psi(X)}\mathbb{E}[\ell(\widehat{Y},Y)].

In particular, a centralized decision rule ψ⁡(X)\psi(X) that has access to XX cannot perform worse than any rule ϕ⁡(Z)\phi(Z) that only sees ZZ.

Proof.

Let UU collect the protocol’s internal randomness, independent of YY, so that Z=g⁡(X,U)Z=g(X,U). Any rule ϕ⁡(Z)\phi(Z) induces a (possibly randomized) rule ψ⁡(X,U):=ϕ⁡(g⁡(X,U))\psi(X,U):=\phi(g(X,U)); hence predictors based on ZZ are a subset of predictors based on (X,U)(X,U) (and thus no better than those based on XX), proving the risk inequality. □\square

Proposition 7 is not an endorsement of star in constrained settings. It is a sanity check: hierarchies are only needed because some constraint makes full centralization infeasible or too expensive. In this paper, the dominant such constraint is the context window WW, which caps the fan-in of any node (Section 2.5). Once WW binds, a star can only incorporate a bounded number of leaves regardless of budget, and that is precisely where hierarchy becomes a meaningful design choice.

5.2 Why chains degrade without new evidence

Chains are appealing in practice because they resemble deliberation: one agent’s output becomes the next agent’s input. However, in our framework a chain does not introduce new independent evidence; it only retransmits and transforms what already exists. Under lossy communication, repeated retransmission compounds loss.

This is explicit in both settings. In the continuous warm-up, (8) shows MSE increases linearly with chain length. In the binary setting, the effect is even simpler.

Proposition 8 (Bias decays along a chain under lossy communication).

Consider a chain of length LL in which a single leaf vote with bias μ0\mu_{0} is transmitted through LL independent communication steps, each with reliability γ⁡(m)\gamma(m), and no new independent evidence enters the chain. Then the final bias is

μchain​(L)=γ​(m)L​μ0.\mu_{\text{chain}}(L)=\gamma(m)^{L}\,\mu_{0}.

Consequently, if γ⁡(m)<1\gamma(m)<1 and L≥1L\geq 1, then μchain​(L)<μ0\mu_{\text{chain}}(L)<\mu_{0}.

Proof.

Each hop multiplies bias by γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) by the channel model in Section 2.3. □\square

Design takeaway.

Absent new evidence, chains are not a mechanism for synergy. If a task is inherently sequential, chains may still be necessary, but then one must model the arrival of new information explicitly. If intermediate agents inject new information or perform error-correcting verification, the effective bias can increase; Proposition 8 isolates the relay-only communication effect. Our phase diagrams therefore focus on star versus tree, which represent the two competing strategies for aggregating many leaf signals under context constraints.

5.3 Context-limited star versus hierarchical trees

The context window WW turns Proposition 7 from a theoretical upper bound into a practical obstacle. A star aggregator that receives NN messages of length mm must read roughly N​mNm tokens, so feasibility requires

N​m≤W⟹N≤Nmax​(m):=⌊Wm⌋.Nm\leq W\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad N\leq N_{\max}(m):=\Big\lfloor\frac{W}{m}\Big\rfloor. (28)

For fixed WW, Nmax​(m)N_{\max}(m) is a constant independent of budget. Thus, once a star uses as many leaves as it can fit in context, additional budget cannot increase the number of incorporated leaves. The only remaining levers are to strengthen each leaf (increase xx) or to increase message length (increase mm) at the cost of reducing Nmax​(m)N_{\max}(m).

A hierarchical tree avoids the global cap (28) by enforcing the context constraint locally. If each internal node has fan-in bb and reads bb messages of length mm, feasibility requires

b​m≤W,bm\leq W, (29)

but the number of leaves can grow as N=bLN=b^{L} with depth LL. In other words, a tree converts a global bottleneck (N​m≤WNm\leq W at one node) into many local bottlenecks (b​m≤Wbm\leq W at many nodes). Figure 7 illustrates this trade-off: the star saturates early due to context limits, while the tree can continue scaling until it reaches its fixed-point ceiling μ⋆\mu^{\star}.

This benefit is real only if information survives the hierarchy. The binary phase transition from Section 4.2 provides the feasibility condition: a deep tree can only maintain nontrivial accuracy when

αρ=γ⁡(m)​(ρ+(1−ρ)​fb′​(0))>1.\alpha_{\rho}=\gamma(m)\big(\rho+(1-\rho)f_{b}^{\prime}(0)\big)>1. (30)

Even when αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1, deeper trees saturate at a fixed point μ⋆\mu^{\star}, so trees should be viewed as a tool for scaling up to a regime of strong performance, not for unlimited improvement.

Figure 8 summarizes the logic in a single picture. A tree can only be useful if it lies above the amplification threshold αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1. Among such trees, budgeted synergy further requires s>βs>\beta, which is equivalent to

s>β⟺αρ>bβ.s>\beta\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\alpha_{\rho}>b^{\beta}. (31)

The next subsection turns (31) into an explicit budget threshold.

5.4 Budget thresholds for synergy: conditions on ss and β\beta

We now connect topology to budget. The question is not whether a deep tree can amplify weak votes in isolation (Section 4), but whether it can do so more efficiently than simply making a single agent stronger. This is where the comparison between the organization exponent ss and the single-agent scaling exponent β\beta becomes decisive.

Setup (growth regime).

We work in the small-signal regime where the single-agent scaling law is well approximated by

μ0​(x)=g⁡(x)≈k​xβ,\mu_{0}(x)=g(x)\approx kx^{\beta},

and where the tree has not yet saturated (so Theorem 5 applies). For a full bb-ary tree of depth LL with N=bLN=b^{L} leaves, the small-signal prediction gives

In Section 4.4 we introduced clipped objectives to account for saturation; when saturation matters, the threshold still indicates whether there exists a budget range in which scale-out should help before the fixed point dominates.

5.5 A universal upper bound on amplification exponents

The organization exponent ss governs how quickly a majority-vote hierarchy can amplify weak signal as the number of leaves grows. It is therefore important to understand its fundamental limits. Perhaps surprisingly, the majority family admits a clean and universal upper bound: no choice of fan-in can make ss exceed 1/21/2 in the binary model with one-bit messages.

Theorem 11 (A universal bound: s≤12s\leq\tfrac{1}{2}).

For every odd b≥3b\geq 3, the majority map satisfies

fb′​(0)≤b.f_{b}^{\prime}(0)\leq\sqrt{b}. (38)

Consequently, for any ρ∈[0,1)\rho\in[0,1) and any γ⁡(m)≤1\gamma(m)\leq 1,

αρ=γ⁡(m)​(ρ+(1−ρ)​fb′​(0))≤b,and hences=log⁡αρlog⁡b≤12.\alpha_{\rho}=\gamma(m)\big(\rho+(1-\rho)f_{b}^{\prime}(0)\big)\leq\sqrt{b},\qquad\text{and hence}\qquad s=\frac{\log\alpha_{\rho}}{\log b}\leq\frac{1}{2}. (39)

Proof sketch.

Equation (38) follows from the closed form fb′​(0)=b​(b−1(b−1)/2)2b−1f_{b}^{\prime}(0)=\frac{b\binom{b-1}{(b-1)/2}}{2^{b-1}} (Lemma 1) and a standard upper bound on the central binomial coefficient. Plugging (38) into (22) yields (39). A fully elementary proof is given in Appendix H. □\square

Implications for synergy.

The bound s≤1/2s\leq 1/2 has two immediate consequences. First, it explains why scale-out is fragile on some tasks. If the single-agent scaling exponent satisfies β≥1/2\beta\geq 1/2, then the inequality s>βs>\beta is impossible under majority-vote hierarchies with one-bit messages. In that regime, a designer should not expect budget-exponent gains from adding agents; improvement must come from making agents stronger, from richer communication than a single bit, or from protocols that effectively reduce shared failures. Second, the bound clarifies the role of diversity. Even if β<1/2\beta<1/2, a large ρ\rho reduces αρ\alpha_{\rho} and pushes ss downward, shrinking or eliminating the synergy region in Figure 8. This is precisely the regime in which practitioners observe that “more agents does not help,” and it suggests a concrete remedy: invest budget not in more of the same agents, but in mechanisms that reduce shared error modes, which in our framework means reducing the effective ρ\rho.

Summary of the phase-diagram logic.

Taken together, the results above reduce topology choice to a few quantitative checks. Under context constraints, deep trees are only viable in the supercritical regime αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1; exponent-level budgeted synergy in the growth range requires s>βs>\beta (equivalently αρ>bβ\alpha_{\rho}>b^{\beta}); and within the majority-vote tree family we always have the universal limit s≤1/2s\leq 1/2. Even when these conditions hold, depth helps only up to saturation: once the recursion is near μ⋆\mu^{\star}, additional budget is typically better spent improving communication fidelity (larger γ⁡(m)\gamma(m)) or reducing shared failures (smaller ρ\rho) than on additional depth. Section 6 turns these checks into a compact design diagnostic within the model.

6 Design Diagnostics Within the Model

The results so far characterize when different organizations can help under a fixed budget: a context-limited star saturates (Section 5.3), chains compound loss (Section 5.2), and trees are viable only in the supercritical regime αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1 with small-signal growth governed by an organization exponent ss (Section 4). Here we translate these results into design diagnostics within the model: given a budget BB, a context window WW, and a small set of effective environment quantities, we ask whether hierarchy is feasible, whether scale-out can outpace scale-up before saturation, and which constraint is binding when it cannot. For LLM-based agent systems, the knobs correspond to token allocations: per-leaf reasoning/compute xx and inter-agent message length mm. The abstraction is deliberately coarse, so the goal is regime prediction and diagnostic guidance, not a faithful end-to-end optimizer for any particular agent stack.

Under a budget BB and context window WW, we parameterize a tree design by

(b,m,x,L)(fan-in, message length, per-leaf compute, depth)(b,\ m,\ x,\ L)\quad\text{(fan-in, message length, per-leaf compute, depth)}

and ask how to choose these quantities to maximize the model-predicted performance subject to feasibility. The inner problem chooses xx for fixed (b,m)(b,m); the outer problem trades off communication quality and coordination cost by selecting (b,m)(b,m) as a function of BB. A key structural takeaway is monotonicity: in the growth regime, the budget-optimal message length can be chosen nondecreasing in BB, yielding efficient design curves rather than expensive search. We focus on binary success/failure tasks, where hierarchies can either amplify or collapse; the continuous setting admits analogous (and smoother) diagnostics via the closed-form recursions of Section 3.

6.1 Closed-form compute allocation: optimal x⋆x^{\star} in the growth regime

Fix a candidate tree architecture specified by a fan-in bb and message length mm, with local feasibility constraint b​m≤Wbm\leq W. Let ρ\rho be the calibrated shared-failure correlation and γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) be the calibrated communication reliability. Define the per-layer weak-signal gain

αρ(b,m):=γ(m)(ρ+(1−ρ)fb′(0)),s(b,m):=log⁡αρ​(b,m)log⁡b(for fixed calibrated ρ).\alpha_{\rho}(b,m):=\gamma(m)\big(\rho+(1-\rho)f_{b}^{\prime}(0)\big),\qquad s(b,m):=\frac{\log\alpha_{\rho}(b,m)}{\log b}\quad\text{(for fixed calibrated }\rho\text{)}.

Theorem 4 implies that deep hierarchies are only viable if αρ​(b,m)>1\alpha_{\rho}(b,m)>1. Assume we are in this supercritical regime and consider budgets for which the system remains in the growth regime before saturation. Under the small-signal scaling approximation g⁡(x)≈k​xβg(x)\approx kx^{\beta} and the tree budget model B≈N⁡(x+c0​(b,m))B\approx N(x+c_{0}(b,m)) with c0​(b,m)=2​m​bb−1c_{0}(b,m)=2m\frac{b}{b-1}, Section 5.4 derived the growth objective

μgrow​(B,b,m,x)≈k​xβ​(Bx+c0​(b,m))s⁡(b,m).\mu_{\mathrm{grow}}(B;b,m,x)\;\approx\;k\,x^{\beta}\left(\frac{B}{x+c_{0}(b,m)}\right)^{s(b,m)}. (40)

A natural design question is whether there is structure in the budget-dependent solution. The answer is yes: in the growth regime, the optimal message length is monotone in the budget. This formalizes a useful heuristic in the model: as you spend more, the optimal design communicates less aggressively compressed information.

6.4 Putting the diagnostics together

We now combine compute allocation, monotone communication design, and saturation into a compact workflow. The inputs are a budget BB, a context window WW, and a small set of estimated effective quantities, in particular μ0​(x)\mu_{0}(x), ρ\rho, and γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) (Section 2.7). The output is a model-based prediction and a set of diagnostics (which constraint is binding), rather than a claim that the abstraction optimizes real agent stacks end-to-end.

Compare against centralization.

For message length mm, a star can include at most Nmax​(m)=⌊W/m⌋N_{\max}(m)=\lfloor W/m\rfloor leaves. When the budget regime of interest does not push beyond this cap, centralization is the natural baseline: it aggregates in one hop and avoids multi-hop loss (Proposition 7). When Nmax​(m)N_{\max}(m) binds, additional budget cannot increase the number of incorporated leaves in a star, and hierarchy becomes the only way to expose more parallel evidence under the same per-node context limit.

Screen tree candidates and allocate compute.

For each odd fan-in b≥3b\geq 3 and each feasible mm with b​m≤Wbm\leq W, compute αρ​(b,m)\alpha_{\rho}(b,m) and s⁡(b,m)s(b,m). Discard candidates with αρ​(b,m)≤1\alpha_{\rho}(b,m)\leq 1, which collapse in depth (Theorem 4). For exponent-level budgeted synergy in the growth regime, also discard s⁡(b,m)≤βs(b,m)\leq\beta. For remaining candidates, set the per-leaf compute to the closed form x⋆​(b,m)x^{\star}(b,m) in (41) (Proposition 12) and choose the implied leaf count and depth via (43), with depth interpreted through the mixing-depth guarantee of Theorem 6. For fixed bb, Algorithm 1 yields the monotone budget-indexed communication curve mb⋆​(B)m_{b}^{\star}(B), so the outer search can be performed efficiently.

In the supercritical regime, the binary recursion converges to a fixed point μ⋆​(b,m)\mu^{\star}(b,m) (computed by iterating u↦fb,ρ​(γ⁡(m)​u)u\mapsto f_{b,\rho}(\gamma(m)u)). To avoid extrapolating the growth law beyond its range, we evaluate a design using the clipped prediction from Section 4.4:

μ^​(B,b,m):=min⁡{μ⋆​(b,m),μ0​(x)​αρ​(b,m)L}.\widehat{\mu}(B;b,m):=\min\big\{\mu^{\star}(b,m),\ \mu_{0}(x)\,\alpha_{\rho}(b,m)^{L}\big\}. (47)

At each budget BB, we compare this clipped tree prediction to the best feasible star and to the single-agent baseline under the same budget.

Interpretation as diagnostics.

These checks separate four common reasons why scaling out fails: context saturation of a star (Nmax​(m)N_{\max}(m) caps centralization), subcriticality (αρ≤1\alpha_{\rho}\leq 1), exponent mismatch (s≤βs\leq\beta), and saturation (μ^\widehat{\mu} close to μ⋆\mu^{\star}). When performance plateaus, the theory points to two levers: improve effective communication fidelity (larger γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) at the same cost) or reduce shared failures (smaller ρ\rho via diversity or verification), rather than increasing depth.

7 Empirical Touchpoints

This paper is primarily theoretical: our goal is to explain why budgeted multi-agent scaling amplifies in some regimes and collapses in others, and to make the relevant regime boundaries explicit. Accordingly, we keep the empirical component modest. We (i) connect our bottlenecks and regime predictions to recent large-scale matched-budget evaluations reported elsewhere, and (ii) provide a minimal synthetic sanity check that recovers the predicted amplification boundary under the assumed model.

7.1 Theoretical Mechanisms in Recent Large-Scale Studies

Large-scale matched-budget evaluations are computationally prohibitive for academic groups, but recent industrial studies provide high-fidelity data that validates our theoretical predictions. Most notably, Kim et al. (2025) conducted an extensive evaluation of scaling laws for agent systems across multiple benchmarks and architectures. Their empirical findings align closely with the qualitative regime boundaries derived in our framework:

  • •

    Context saturation and coordination overhead. Kim et al. (2025) observe that simply concatenating agent traces can degrade performance on tool-heavy tasks when coordination overhead consumes the context window. In our framework, this corresponds to the N​m≤WNm\leq W bottleneck: once a centralized aggregator becomes context-saturated, adding agents can dilute usable signal.

  • •

    Saturation at strong baselines. They report diminishing (and sometimes negative) returns once the single-agent baseline is already strong. This is consistent with our fixed-point analysis: once a hierarchy approaches its saturation point μ⋆\mu^{\star}, marginal gains from adding depth or leaves are small; improvement requires changing effective parameters (better γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) or smaller ρ\rho), not more aggregation.

  • •

    Shared failures and error cascades. They emphasize that agents can share failure modes and that naive aggregation can amplify errors, while more structured coordination can mitigate this. In our framework, shared failures are summarized by ρ\rho: higher ρ\rho pushes αρ\alpha_{\rho} downward and can drive hierarchies into the subcritical regime where depth washes out information.

By providing the mathematical derivation for these empirically observed regimes, our theory explains why scaling fails when it does, suggesting that future improvements must come from altering the effective parameters, specifically increasing γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) or decreasing ρ\rho, rather than simply adding more agents.

7.2 Synthetic sanity check: recovering the amplification boundary

Synthetic experiments provide a controlled setting where the ground-truth parameters are known and the phase boundary can be probed directly. Our goal here is not to optimize absolute performance, but to verify that the qualitative prediction—amplification versus collapse governed by αρ\alpha_{\rho}—is recovered under the generative model analyzed in Section 4.

We include one lightweight Monte Carlo study under the ρ\rho-shared binary model. We fix b=5b=5, γ=0.6\gamma=0.6, μ0=0.05\mu_{0}=0.05, sweep ρ∈[0,0.8]\rho\in[0,0.8], and compare the recursion prediction μL\mu_{L} at depths L∈{10,30}L\in\{10,30\} to Monte Carlo estimates (n=50,000n=50{,}000). Figure 11 shows close agreement and a sharpening transition around the predicted boundary αρ=1\alpha_{\rho}=1.

For continuous tasks, the same role can be played by a simple correlated-Gaussian generator, where the closed-form expressions of Section 3.2 make correlation and communication floors explicit.

8 Discussion and Limitations

We asked when scaling out a budgeted multi-agent system yields synergy and when it fails. The framework is intentionally minimal: it treats an agent as a black-box solver with an allocated compute budget, models inter-agent communication as a controllable lossy channel, and summarizes shared failures through an effective correlation parameter. This minimalism makes the regime boundaries transparent, but it also defines what the theory does and does not claim.

8.1 Relationship to prior results

Our binary phase transition echoes reconstruction thresholds for broadcasting on trees (Kesten and Stigum, 1966; Evans et al., 2000; Mossel, 2001), where information can or cannot propagate from leaves to the root depending on a single scalar. Two differences are central for agent-system design. First, our “channel” is partly under design control: message length trades off fidelity γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) against budget and context constraints, so the relevant threshold depends on an explicit communication choice. Second, we couple propagation to a fixed-budget allocation problem: an amplifiable hierarchy is synergistic only when its organization exponent outpaces single-agent scaling.

Recent work offers complementary perspectives on information flow in agent systems. He et al. (2025) cast agentic architectures as compressor–predictor pairs and propose mutual information between context and compression as a task-independent proxy for information survival; their finding that scaling the compressor can dominate scaling the predictor aligns with our emphasis on communication fidelity γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) as a first-order bottleneck, though our framework adds explicit budget constraints and multi-hop aggregation structure. Li (2026) study skill selection in single-agent systems and observe a phase transition: selection accuracy remains stable up to a critical library size then drops sharply, with semantic confusability among skills playing a central role. This echoes our amplification–collapse dichotomy, but at a different interface: where we model information loss across agents, they model selection confusion within a single agent’s skill routing. Together, these results suggest that sharp thresholds, whether in inter-agent communication, intra-agent skill selection, or hierarchical aggregation, may be a recurring motif in bounded-resource AI systems.

8.2 What the framework explains (and what it does not)

The framework is designed to explain qualitative regime changes that are otherwise hard to diagnose: why stars saturate under context limits, why chains compound loss, why trees can either amplify or collapse depending on αρ\alpha_{\rho}, and why correlated failures impose floors that make large ensembles behave like “one agent with shared blind spots.” It also clarifies what additional sophistication must accomplish: any useful complexity must effectively increase communication fidelity, reduce shared failures, or relax the fan-in constraint.

At the same time, the model is not a faithful simulator of real agent stacks. Parameters such as ρ\rho and γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) are effective summaries that can vary with depth, prompts, tools, and task difficulty; real communication is far richer than a one-bit abstraction; and practical budget accounting can differ across implementations. For these reasons, we view the theory as a coordination diagnostic—predicting which constraint is binding and which direction should help—rather than as a source of precise point predictions. Crucially, the alignment between our derived bottlenecks and independent large-scale observations (Kim et al., 2025) suggests that the effective parameters defined here capture the structural essence of the scaling problem, rendering the theory robust to changes in the underlying base models.

8.3 How stronger protocols fit the framework

Protocols such as debate, critique, verification, or self-consistency can be interpreted as mechanisms that change the effective parameters of the model (Irving et al., 2018; Christiano et al., 2018; Du et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2023). For example, structured verification can reduce effective shared failures (ρ\rho), while richer message schemas can improve effective fidelity (γ⁡(m)\gamma(m)); both, however, typically increase coordination cost. The theory suggests a concrete way to evaluate such protocols: measure how much they move the effective bottlenecks per unit budget, and check whether they move the system across the supercritical boundary αρ>1\alpha_{\rho}>1 or the synergy boundary s>βs>\beta.

8.4 Extensions beyond our scope

Several extensions are natural. Allowing heterogeneity across leaves (different models, prompts, or tools) makes ρ\rho and scaling task- and agent-dependent; a tractable next step is to treat ρ\rho as depth-dependent or to model mixtures of agent types. More general graphs and multi-round interaction can be analyzed by unrolling protocols into computation graphs, but doing so requires accounting for how added edges change effective dependence as well as cost. Finally, our strongest binary bounds rely on one-bit-style messages and majority aggregation; allowing richer messages or confidence reports changes the amplification map and may relax universal exponent limits. In all cases, the guiding principle remains the same: additional structure helps only insofar as it relaxes the binding constraints (context, communication loss, or shared failures) under a fixed budget.

9 Conclusion

Multi-agent systems can exhibit synergy, but under a fixed budget scaling out is not monotone: it can help, saturate, or collapse. We argued that these outcomes become predictable once we make the binding constraints explicit: finite context windows, lossy communication, and shared failures, and summarize an environment by a small set of measurable effective parameters.

In a continuous warm-up we derived closed-form risks for star/chain/tree organizations and exposed correlation and communication floors. For binary success/failure tasks, we proved a sharp amplification–collapse phase transition for deep majority trees and characterized the resulting fixed-point saturation and mixing depth. In the amplifying regime we introduced an organization exponent ss governing small-signal growth and showed that budgeted synergy in the growth range occurs exactly when s>βs>\beta, yielding closed-form compute allocation and explicit budget thresholds. We also translated these results into simple design diagnostics within the model.

The broader message is that topology is not magic. Hierarchies are useful because context limits can make full centralization infeasible, and they succeed only when communication is sufficiently faithful and shared failures are sufficiently weak. We hope this work helps move agent-system design from ad hoc heuristics toward principled, testable coordination theories.

I.2 Upper-envelope construction and correctness of Algorithm 1

We sketch a standard correctness argument for the stack-based envelope construction used in Algorithm 1. Consider a finite family of lines ℓi​(t)=si​t+qi\ell_{i}(t)=s_{i}t+q_{i} with strictly increasing slopes s1<s2<⋯<sMs_{1}<s_{2}<\cdots<s_{M}. Define the upper envelope E⁡(t)=maxi⁡ℓi​(t)E(t)=\max_{i}\ell_{i}(t).

Lemma 20 (Envelope structure for increasing slopes).

If sis_{i} are strictly increasing, then there exist indices 1≤i1<i2<⋯<ir≤M1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<\cdots<i_{r}\leq M and breakpoints −∞=τ0<τ1<⋯<τr=∞-\infty=\tau_{0}<\tau_{1}<\cdots<\tau_{r}=\infty such that for every j∈{1,…,r}j\in\{1,\dots,r\},

E⁡(t)=ℓij​(t)for all ​t∈[τj−1,τj).E(t)=\ell_{i_{j}}(t)\quad\text{for all }t\in[\tau_{j-1},\tau_{j}).

That is, the maximizing index is nondecreasing in tt and changes only at increasing intersection points.

Proof.

For any pair i<ji<j, the difference ℓj​(t)−ℓi​(t)\ell_{j}(t)-\ell_{i}(t) is an increasing affine function of tt (because sj−si>0s_{j}-s_{i}>0). Therefore, the set where ℓj\ell_{j} dominates ℓi\ell_{i} is either empty or a half-line [t⋆,∞)[t^{\star},\infty), where t⋆t^{\star} is their intersection. This single-crossing property implies the argmax index over {ℓi}\{\ell_{i}\} is nondecreasing in tt, and the envelope is piecewise linear with breakpoints at pairwise intersections. ∎

Algorithm 1 is a constructive implementation of Lemma 20. Processing lines in increasing slope order, it maintains a stack of candidate lines (ℓi1,…,ℓir)(\ell_{i_{1}},\dots,\ell_{i_{r}}) and the associated increasing breakpoints (τ1,…,τr−1)(\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{r-1}). When a new line ℓ\ell is added, if its intersection with the current top occurs to the left of the top’s activation breakpoint, then the top line is never maximal and is removed. Because each line is pushed and popped at most once, the construction runs in linear time. The resulting stack and breakpoint list exactly encode the envelope E⁡(t)E(t), and the associated maximizing message length is the piecewise-constant function mb⋆​(B)m_{b}^{\star}(B) in Theorem 13.

Appendix J Calibration and evaluation templates

This appendix collects optional templates for estimating the effective parameters of the framework in a given agent stack and for running small diagnostic evaluations. Because the main paper is theoretical and the modeling assumptions are deliberately simplified, these templates are intended primarily to support qualitative regime checks (e.g., whether αρ\alpha_{\rho} is supercritical, or whether saturation is communication- versus correlation-limited), rather than to provide a faithful simulator of all real-world effects.

J.1 Calibration protocol: estimating β\beta, γ⁡(m)\gamma(m) / σc2​(m)\sigma_{c}^{2}(m), and ρ\rho

This subsection operationalizes the “measurable parameters” promise from Section 2.7. The goal is not to fit a complicated model, but to obtain stable estimates that are accurate enough to place the system in the correct qualitative regime of the phase diagram.

Single-agent scaling (β\beta).

Fix a leaf-agent template (model, prompt, tools) and define a compute knob xx (e.g., reasoning tokens, number of samples, number of tool calls). Evaluate the leaf agent on calibration tasks at a grid x1<⋯<xKx_{1}<\cdots<x_{K} (roughly log-spaced).

For binary tasks, estimate accuracy p^​(xk)\widehat{p}(x_{k}) and convert to bias μ^​(xk)=2​p^​(xk)−1\widehat{\mu}(x_{k})=2\widehat{p}(x_{k})-1. Fit a power law on a small-signal window where μ^\widehat{\mu} is positive and not saturated, e.g.,

log⁡μ^​(xk)≈log⁡k+β​log⁡xk,k∈𝒦,\log\widehat{\mu}(x_{k})\approx\log k+\beta\log x_{k},\qquad k\in\mathcal{K},

For binary tasks, sample Y∈{−1,+1}Y\in\{-1,+1\} uniformly, ask a sender to encode YY into at most mm tokens, and ask a receiver to decode Y^\widehat{Y} from the message alone. The empirical flip rate ϵ^​(m)=Pr⁡(Y^≠Y)\widehat{\epsilon}(m)=\Pr(\widehat{Y}\neq Y) yields γ^​(m)=1−2​ϵ^​(m)\widehat{\gamma}(m)=1-2\widehat{\epsilon}(m). Finally, record realized costs: tokens generated and tokens read (including system prompts, tool outputs, and formatting overhead), and verify the effective context window WW after templating.
